revisionTopics.reason: 3 days since review · Missed on Quiz 4

flashcards.front: When do two operations O_i(x) and O_j(x) in a schedule S conflict?
flashcards.back: They belong to different transactions (T_i ≠ T_j), access the exact same data item x, and at least one of the operations is a Write(x).

flashcards.front: How do you prove a schedule S is conflict serializable using a Precedence Graph?
flashcards.back: Construct a directed graph where nodes are transactions and edge T_i → T_j exists if an operation in T_i precedes and conflicts with one in T_j. S is conflict serializable iff the precedence graph has NO cycles.

flashcards.front: Can T2: R(A) be swapped past T1: W(A) in schedule S1?
flashcards.back: No. R(A) and W(A) on the same item A from different transactions form a Read-Write (RW) conflict. Swapping them changes the value read by T2.

flashcards.front: Contrast Wait-Die vs. Wound-Wait timestamp schemes for deadlock prevention.
flashcards.back: Wait-Die is non-preemptive: older transaction waits for younger, younger dies (aborts) if requesting held lock. Wound-Wait is preemptive: older transaction wounds (preempts) younger, while younger is allowed to wait for older.

flashcards.front: How can the "Hold and Wait" Coffman condition be eliminated?
flashcards.back: Require a process/transaction to request and be allocated all required resources atomically before execution begins, or allow it to request resources only when it currently holds none.

flashcards.front: Why is Strict 2PL preferred over Basic 2PL in production database engines?
flashcards.back: Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but remains vulnerable to cascading rollbacks. Strict 2PL holds all exclusive (write) locks until Commit/Abort, ensuring both serializability and cascadeless schedules.

materials.title: NoteNest Problem Statement
materials.subject: dsa
materials.excerptText: "Students struggle with fragmented study materials scattered across PDFs, slides, and handwritten notes, leading to passive reading and poor exam retention. NoteNest unifies subject-organized document management, grounded AI topic summarization, and active recall flashcards."
materials.fullSummary: NoteNest Problem Statement: Engineering and university students face severe information fragmentation across lecture PDFs, slides, and notes, resulting in last-minute cramming and low retention. NoteNest solves this by providing a centralized subject-wise repository, instant document-grounded AI topic summaries, interactive Q&A with citations, and spaced-repetition flashcards.
materials.rawContent:
NoteNest Problem Statement

1. Executive Problem Overview
University students manage dozens of heterogeneous study artifacts across multiple courses every semester—including lecture PDFs, slide decks, handwritten class notes, and textbook excerpts. Because these materials remain scattered across local folders and messaging apps, students spend excessive time searching for concepts rather than understanding them.

2. Core Student Pain Points
- Material Fragmentation: Notes and PDFs are not organized by subject hierarchy or mapped to syllabus topics.
- Passive Reading Trap: Re-reading dense 40-page PDFs creates an illusion of competence without testing active recall.
- Generic Unverified AI Answers: General-purpose chatbots hallucinate or give off-syllabus answers that do not match professor lecture notes.
- Lack of Revision Prioritization: Students lack visibility into which topics have low retention before exams.

3. Proposed Solution: NoteNest Architecture
- Subject-Wise Document Repository: Structured folders per course with instant PDF/document viewing, search, and topic organization.
- Grounded AI Topic Summarizer: Generates executive overviews, key takeaways, core definitions, exam high-yield tips, and self-check Q&As strictly grounded in uploaded files.
- Active Recall & Flashcard Engine: Converts document concepts into interactive flashcards and quizzes to track mastery.

Replaces passive re-reading with instant AI-synthesized topic summaries, key definitions, and high-yield exam takeaways grounded in the student's own files.
Prevents AI hallucination and off-syllabus confusion through strict document grounding and verifiable section citations.
Bridges the gap between reading and retention by automatically generating self-check questions and active recall flashcards per document.

AI synthesis restricted strictly to the student's uploaded study material so definitions and takeaways align with the course syllabus.

Hierarchical workspace where each academic subject maintains its own documents, AI summaries, and mastery metrics.

examHighYieldPoints: Focus on the 3-pillar workflow: Organize by Subject -> Summarize Topic with Grounded AI -> Reinforce via Active Recall Flashcards.
Contrast passive review (re-reading PDFs) against active recall (self-check Q&As and spaced repetition).
Highlight how document-level AI scoping prevents cross-subject confusion.

materials.rawContent:
NoteNest User Research & User Journey Mapping

1. User Research Objectives & Methodology
Conducted contextual inquiries and surveys with undergraduate engineering and science students to understand how they collect, read, summarize, and revise study materials before midterms and finals.

2. Primary Student Personas
- The Overwhelmed Exam Crammer: Has 15+ unread lecture PDFs across 5 subjects days before the exam; needs instant high-yield topic summaries and exam tips.
- The Structured Synthesizer: Organizes notes weekly by subject and wants a unified workspace to view PDFs, extract definitions, and test recall.

3. Five-Stage User Journey Map
- Stage 1: Subject Setup & Onboarding — Student creates profile, selects semester subjects, and establishes study goals.
- Stage 2: Document Ingestion & Viewing — Student uploads course PDFs into specific subjects and views/searches documents directly in-app.
- Stage 3: AI Topic Summarization — Student clicks Summarize Topic beside any document to generate structured overviews, definitions, and exam tips.
- Stage 4: Contextual Q&A Verification — Student asks targeted questions in the AI Study Assistant scoped to selected subject PDFs.
- Stage 5: Active Recall & Mastery — Student reviews auto-generated flashcards and quizzes to boost retention scores.

Identifies critical UX friction points in existing tools: hidden actions, inability to preview uploaded PDFs in-place, and confusing cross-subject navigation.
Establishes clear design solutions: placing View Document, Summarize Topic, and Delete actions directly beside every file inside each subject and search bar.
